back: Not a separate domain: sourcing is planned in Governance (Plan Sourcing Strategy); procurement is explained in Appendix X4.
Buyer and seller know different things about the deal; a source of procurement risk.
Plan (needs, documents, sellers); conduct (bids, selection, negotiation, award); monitor and control (performance, changes, closing).
Documents sourcing decisions, the source selection approach, the scope of external work, and the contracts and sources: what, how and when to acquire.
Sourcing strategy plan: insourcing or outsourcing decisions and source selection criteria.
Compares making internally with buying; may use payback, ROI, IRR, NPV or cost-benefit analysis, and weighs the risks.
Uses internal expertise; often cheaper for substantial innovation; tighter strategic integration; more control.
External expertise; often cheaper for common goods; frees capacity and capital; transfers delivery risk; keeps supplier relations.
Sets the delivery method, the type of legally binding agreement, and the procurement phases.
Multiparty agreement; shared risks and rewards; early involvement; collaborative decisions; open-book accounting.
RFI: market information before bidding. RFP: complex scope, vendor proposes a solution. RFQ: price decides, solution readily available.
A meeting after the bid documents go out, to answer all bidders' questions with the same information.
For standard, routine work with a well-defined outcome; avoid it for complex procurements.
Only one supplier can meet the requirement (patents, exclusive rights); not a way to favor a vendor.
The budget is disclosed and the best proposal within it wins; only for a precise SOW with no changes expected.
Capability, life cycle cost, delivery dates, technical approach, experience, key staff, financial stability, sustainability; weighted to rank proposals.
Set fee for a defined scope; cost risk on the seller; budget certainty for the buyer, possibly with a risk premium.
Actual costs plus a fee; for uncertain scope or high risk; cost risk on the buyer.
A hybrid: pays actual time and materials plus a margin; for small jobs, experts, unclear scope; needs close monitoring.
Firm fixed price; fixed price incentive fee (with a price ceiling); fixed price with economic price adjustment (long contracts, other currencies).
Cost plus fixed fee; cost plus incentive fee (savings and overruns shared, e.g. 80/20); cost plus award fee (buyer's subjective judgment).
Multitiered structure, value-driven payments, fixed-price increments, not-to-exceed T&M, graduated T&M, early cancellation, dynamic scope, team augmentation.
A procurement team member with authority to sign contracts; the project manager may attend to assist.
A contested change: the parties disagree on compensation or on whether a change happened. Negotiation is the preferred way to settle it.
Negotiation, mediation, dispute review board, expert determination, arbitration (binding); litigation is the last option.
